questions.q: What is the correct definition of the complex inner product <psi|phi> for vectors psi and phi in C^n?
options: The sum of psi_i-conjugate times phi_i, for i = 1 to n
The sum of psi_i times phi_i-conjugate, for i = 1 to n
The product of ||psi|| and ||phi|| only, ignoring the individual components
The sum of psi_i times phi_i, with no conjugation
questions.explain: The complex inner product conjugates the entries of the first vector before multiplying: <psi|phi> = sum of psi_i* phi_i. Conjugating the other vector's entries instead would give <phi|psi>, not <psi|phi>.
Term by term: (1-i)(3) = 3 - 3i, and (2+i)(1+2i) = 0 + 5i. Summing gives (3-3i) + (0+5i) = 3 + 2i.

questions.q: Why is <phi|psi> generally NOT equal to <psi|phi> for complex vectors?
options: The two expressions are always equal, just like the real dot product
Inner products are undefined when the vectors have complex entries
<phi|psi> is always zero regardless of the vectors involved
Swapping the order conjugates the result: <phi|psi> = <psi|phi>*, so the two are equal only when the inner product is real
questions.explain: Unlike the real dot product, the complex inner product is conjugate-symmetric rather than symmetric: <phi|psi> = <psi|phi>*. They coincide only when the inner product happens to be a real number.

questions.q: Why does the inner product definition conjugate the first vector's entries before multiplying, rather than leaving them unconjugated?
options: It is a historical convention with no mathematical consequence
It converts every complex vector into a real vector before any arithmetic happens
It guarantees <psi|psi> = sum of |psi_i|^2, which is always real and non-negative, so a meaningful norm (length) can be defined for complex vectors
It makes the inner product of any two vectors always equal to zero
questions.explain: Without the conjugate, <psi|psi> could come out complex or negative, making 'length' meaningless. With it, each term becomes |psi_i|^2, which is always a non-negative real number.

questions.q: Why is a finite-dimensional complex vector space like C^2, equipped with this inner product, automatically a Hilbert space?
options: Because the vectors in C^2 all happen to have norm exactly 1
Because Hilbert spaces are defined as having exactly two dimensions
A Hilbert space needs an inner product plus completeness (no missing limit points), and finite-dimensional spaces have no room for such gaps, so completeness is automatic
Because C^2 only contains real numbers, which simplifies the completeness requirement
questions.explain: Completeness means there are no 'gaps' where a converging sequence of vectors lacks a limit inside the space. Finite dimensions guarantee this automatically, so any finite-dimensional complex inner product space qualifies as a Hilbert space with no extra work.
